Grepped `cached(` across lib/services/*.ts myself: it is used in admin.service.ts, admin-geography.service.ts, analytics.service.ts and organization-finance.service.ts — zero hits in accounting.service.ts, confirming none of these 9 reports is cached. verified.title: withDb() spends 5 network round trips of pure transaction/context overhead before every call — 3 separate set_config calls that collapse into 1
verified.evidence: Read lib/db/index.ts myself: setTenantLocals (:121-131 in the finder's citation; I read it at the equivalent location in the current file) issues 3 sequentially-awaited `SELECT set_config($1,$2,TRUE)` calls (4 when organizationId is set), and withDb (same file) wraps every call in an explicit BEGIN...COMMIT — so every withDb() invocation costs 5 round trips of pure overhead regardless of how many real statements run inside it. I could not re-run pg_stat_statements myself this session, but a sibling verifier (api-routes-and-the-service-layer.json, live SQL against the same production project on 2026-09-05) independently measured `SELECT set_config($1, $2, $3)` = 6,591 calls and a differently-normalized form = 6,409 calls, 13,000 total, 800ms combined server-side exec time over a 121-day pg_stat_statements window — matching this finding's cited 6,591/6,409/346ms/454ms figures exactly. That same sibling audit computed ~36 tenant DB transactions/day platform-wide from that count (13,000 calls ÷ 3 set_config-per-transaction ÷ 121 days), which tempers the urgency of the AGGREGATE server-side cost (800ms in 4 months is trivial) without invalidating this finding's actual claim, which is about PER-REQUEST latency added to a single /accounting or /dashboard page load, not aggregate server load — that math (9-10 withDb() calls × 2 saved round trips = 18-20 fewer round trips per page view) is unaffected by how often the page is loaded. I confirmed vercel.json contains only `{"buildCommand": "npm run build"}`, no `regions` key, exactly as claimed.
verified.impact: Confirmed as a real, mergeable overhead on every withDb() call. The specific 'ms of latency' impact figures depend on an RTT I cannot measure (same caveat the finder themselves flagged), but the round-trip COUNT is deterministic from the code and the merge is safe (the three set_config calls are independent and already parameterised). Real-world urgency is tempered by corroborated low traffic (~36 tenant transactions/day platform-wide as of 9 days ago) — this is a real but currently low-stakes optimization, not an active production bottleneck.
verified.recommendation: Same as finder's: collapse the three (four) set_config calls into one multi-argument statement inside setTenantLocals. Confirming/pinning the Vercel function region remains valid advice but unverifiable by me this session.
verified.note: Structural mechanism confirmed by direct code read. Numeric pg_stat_statements figures could not be re-run by me this session but are independently corroborated to the exact digit by a sibling verifier's live-SQL run against the same production database 9 days earlier.

verified.title: Query planning costs 8-25x execution on the group surface — 802 shared buffers touched per plan, and node-pg re-plans every statement
verified.evidence: I could not re-run the cited EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) against live prod this session (Supabase tool unavailable platform-wide today), so the specific 13.4ms/2.27ms planning-time and 801/802/655-buffer figures are unverified by me and carried forward from the finder without independent reproduction. What I could and did check: the top-line catalog-size claim ('SELECT count(*) FROM pg_class WHERE relkind=\'i\'' = 1,253 indexes, relkind='r' = 255 tables) has no schema filter, meaning it necessarily includes PostgreSQL/Supabase's own system-catalog indexes and tables (pg_catalog, information_schema-backed objects, TOAST tables) that exist in every Postgres database regardless of this application's schema design. A sibling verifier (postgres-schema-indexing-and-storage-eff.json) independently ran live SQL against the SAME production project 9 days earlier and found only 478 indexes in the public schema and ~926 across ALL non-system schemas combined — nowhere near 1,253. The 278-policy figure is closer to that same sibling's independently-confirmed 276 (small drift over 9 days is expected). Framing 1,253 as 'the schema's indexes' that 'the group surface pays for' therefore folds in roughly 300+ objects that have nothing to do with this application's own index design. I separately reconstructed the six 'permanently-empty' tables' index counts directly from every CREATE TABLE/CREATE INDEX statement in supabase/migrations/*.sql (the only path these objects are ever created through): meeting_attendance = 9 (1 PK + 1 UNIQUE(meeting_id,member_id) + 3 from migration 023 + 2 from 024 + 2 from 068) vs the finder's 8; meeting_resolutions = 8 (1 PK + 2 from 023 + 2 from 024 + 3 from 068) vs the finder's 7; share_transactions ≈ 12-13 (1 PK + 6 from migration 036 + 4 from 068 + 1 from 057 + 1 from 121) vs the finder's 12 — close; investment_returns = 6 (1 PK + 3 from 022 + 2 from 024 + 1 from 068) vs the finder's 5; investment_expenses = 4 (1 PK + 3 from migration 156) vs the finder's 4 — exact. The one real discrepancy: member_investment_shares — I read its sole CREATE TABLE (migration 072b) plus every later migration that references it (only migration 068 adds one more index) and found exactly 3 indexes total (the id PK, the UNIQUE(investment_id, member_id) constraint, and idx_member_investment_shares_group_id), not 5 as claimed. The 'no writer' claim for that table I independently confirmed via grep: zero `INSERT INTO ... member_investment_shares` anywhere in lib/ or app/.
verified.impact: The underlying mechanism (small/empty tables still carrying real index weight; a schema whose catalog is disproportionate to its ~37-group_members/23-contributions live dataset) is real and independently plausible, and the empty-table index counts I could reconstruct from DDL land in the same rough magnitude the finder cited (mostly matching or slightly exceeding their per-table counts, one exact match on investment_expenses) — except member_investment_shares, which the finder overstated by 5 vs an actual 3. The headline '1,253 indexes / 255 tables' framing is the larger overstatement: it is very likely a whole-cluster count that includes hundreds of built-in Postgres/Supabase system objects, not a measure of this application's own schema bloat, and the comparable, independently-verified same-project figure is 478 (public schema) to 926 (all non-system schemas) — 26-46% of the cited number. The specific EXPLAIN ANALYZE timing/buffer numbers are unverified this session.
verified.recommendation: The recommendation to drop indexes on genuinely-empty, writerless tables (member_investment_shares chief among them, which finding #10 independently identifies as dead) remains sound advice regardless of the exact index count. Before acting on the '1,253 indexes' framing specifically, re-run the catalog-size query restricted to non-system schemas (`WHERE schemaname NOT IN ('pg_catalog','information_schema')`) to get the number that actually reflects this application's own schema design.
verified.note: Downgraded from CONFIRMED to OVERSTATED because the two headline catalog-size numbers this finding's title and impact lean on (1,253 indexes, 255 tables) are contradicted by a sibling verifier's live-SQL measurement on the same production database (478-926 range) and almost certainly conflate system-catalog objects with application schema bloat; one of the six per-table index counts (member_investment_shares) is also overstated (5 claimed vs 3 actual, verified against every migration that ever touches that table). The core empty-table-bloat mechanism and the EXPLAIN-plan-shape claim (no cached plan; unnamed extended-protocol statements, confirmed via grep — zero named-statement usage anywhere in lib/db) are still credible.

verified.title: members.service.list ships all 30 columns including password_hash and reset_otp_hash, then strips them in JavaScript
verified.evidence: Confirmed `m.*` at members.service.ts:153 and `SELECT * FROM accounts` at accounting.service.ts:252 exactly as cited. Confirmed password_hash/reset_otp_hash/reset_otp_expires_at/reset_otp_attempts/session_version all exist as real columns on `members` (migration 20260730000000_104_password_reset_otp.sql adds the reset_otp_* columns; grepped the whole migrations directory to confirm). BUT: I read the actual `stripSecrets()` function (members.service.ts:98-101) and it is typed and implemented to strip ONLY `password_hash` — `const { password_hash: _secret, ...rest } = row; return rest;`. I then read `applyMemberMask()` (lib/utils/mask.ts:21-38) and confirmed it masks only phone/email/national_id/date_of_birth/address for PII purposes — it never touches reset_otp_hash, reset_otp_expires_at, reset_otp_attempts, or session_version. I then read `ok()` (lib/utils/response.ts:7-9): `NextResponse.json({success:true, data})` — a plain JSON.stringify of whatever object shape reaches it, with no field allowlist. Conclusion: contrary to this finding's own evidence text ('They are removed after the fact... via stripSecrets(applyMemberMask(...))'), only password_hash is actually removed — reset_otp_hash, reset_otp_expires_at, reset_otp_attempts and session_version ARE currently serialized to the client on every GET /members and GET /members/:id response, for any authenticated fellow member of the same group (the route uses `withAuth`, not an elevated permission — app/api/v1/members/route.ts:8-9). I traced how reset_otp_hash is produced: lib/services/group-verification.service.ts:28-29 `hashSecret()` is unsalted `crypto.createHash('sha256').update(secret).digest('hex')`, and `generateOtp()` (:36-38) produces a 6-digit code via `crypto.randomInt(100_000, 1_000_000)` — 900,000 possibilities. lib/services/password-reset.service.ts confirms reset_otp_hash is looked up by exact-equality (`WHERE reset_otp_hash = $1` pattern in admin-password-reset.service.ts:83) and that resetPasswordWithOtp's 5-attempt limit (MAX_OTP_ATTEMPTS, password-reset.service.ts:22) is enforced only against ONLINE guesses through that endpoint — it does nothing to stop an attacker who has already recovered the plaintext OTP by brute-forcing the leaked SHA-256 hash offline (900,000 SHA-256 computations take well under a second on ordinary hardware), then calling resetPasswordWithOtp once with the correct value.
verified.impact: Substantially worse than this finding characterized it. This is not 'a wide-row read that is a security smell, one refactor away from leaking' — for reset_otp_hash specifically it is a live, currently-exploitable account-takeover chain: any authenticated member of a group can call GET /members (an ordinary, permission-light action every member can already perform) and receive every fellow group member's live password-reset-OTP hash whenever one is mid-reset (a 10-minute window per request, OTP_TTL_MINUTES=10 in password-reset.service.ts:21), brute-force the 6-digit OTP offline in under a second, then take over that member's account via resetPasswordWithOtp — bypassing the endpoint's 5-attempt rate limit entirely since the guess is made offline, not through the API. session_version (used to invalidate all of a user's existing sessions on password change) is also exposed, though its exploitation value is unclear without a companion vulnerability.
verified.recommendation: Immediate: extend stripSecrets (or replace the m.* SELECT with an explicit column list, as the finder recommended) to also remove reset_otp_hash, reset_otp_expires_at, reset_otp_attempts, and session_version — not just password_hash — from every response the members service returns (list, getById, and the two other call sites at :273 and :327 that call stripSecrets alone without this additional exposure fixed). This should be treated as a security incident requiring prompt patching, not a routine optimization backlog item — recommend confirming with the user whether any group has had an active password-reset window observed by another member, and consider invalidating all outstanding reset_otp_hash values as a precaution once patched.
verified.note: The finder correctly identified that sensitive columns cross the network via `m.*`, but their own evidence text ('removed after the fact... via stripSecrets(applyMemberMask(...))') is factually wrong for 4 of the 5 columns they listed, and they characterized the whole thing as 'low' severity. I traced the actual masking/stripping code and found only password_hash is removed; the other four fields, including an OTP-reset hash that is trivially reversible offline, are live in the JSON response today. Reclassified severity from low to critical and rewrote evidence/impact to describe the real, exploitable account-takeover chain I found and verified in the source (unsalted SHA-256 of a 6-digit code, looked up by exact match, with no offline-brute-force protection).

verified.title: The meetings list has no index for its default sort and fiscal_periods has no LIMIT at all
verified.evidence: Could not re-run the cited EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) myself this session (no live SQL access), but independently reconstructed the index situation from every migration that ever touches `meetings`: grepped the full migrations directory for every `ON public.meetings(...)` index definition and found exactly what the finder describes — `idx_meetings_group_status_scheduled ON meetings (group_id, status, scheduled_at ASC)` (migration 024) has status as its 2nd key column, so it cannot serve an unfiltered `WHERE group_id=$1 ORDER BY scheduled_at DESC` via an ordered index scan; `idx_meetings_group_created ON meetings (group_id, created_at DESC)` sorts a different column entirely; and no other index in any migration combines group_id with scheduled_at as an immediate second key — confirmed by grepping every `ON public.meetings` occurrence across the whole migrations directory (10 total index definitions found, none matching). Read meetings.service.ts:102/112 myself: `ORDER BY m.scheduled_at DESC` with no status filter by default, exactly as cited. Confirmed fiscal-periods.service.ts:29-32 is `SELECT * FROM fiscal_periods WHERE group_id = $1 ORDER BY period_start DESC` with no LIMIT anywhere, matching exactly, and confirmed it's consumed by the always-on useFiscalPeriods hook (finding #1's evidence).
verified.impact: Confirmed as a real coverage gap. The finder's own caveat ('neither is urgent at 2 meetings and 0 fiscal periods') is consistent with what I found: the single-column meetings_scheduled_at_idx and meetings_group_id_idx (migration 023) DO both exist, so Postgres has index options even without the ideal composite — at current tiny table sizes a Seq Scan is likely genuinely cheaper regardless, which is why the finder correctly did not claim urgency.
verified.recommendation: Same as finder's: add the composite (group_id, scheduled_at DESC) index and a LIMIT on fiscal-periods.service.ts:29.
verified.note: The missing-composite-index claim was independently reconstructed from migration DDL (a fully deterministic source, since these files are the only way indexes are ever created in this codebase) rather than from live EXPLAIN output, which I could not re-run this session.
